surfaces.part: glowing lit panels in the back wall

answer.evidence: The main body is a staircase that descends into a dark opening, framed by a lintel and side pillars. Each step has a light front-edge line (rows 19, 23, 28, 34, 40) followed by a 2-4 row tread and then 2 rows of dark shadow (rows 21-22, 26-27, 32-33, 38-39, 45-46). The treads therefore read as horizontal surfaces seen from above, and they get wider and taller toward the bottom. The frame is mostly vertical faces. The lintel is only a 3-row strip (light row 1, dark row 2) with no real top slope. The overall impression is a front face with stepped top surfaces, so it reads as three-quarter, though weakly.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small stairs-down prop (a wooden stairwell with steps), not a whole building with roof, walls and door/windows, so it does not match the reference kind. Judged on craft anyway: it has only about 3 lightness steps on the wood, a dark, nearly neutral outline around the frame (81% of dark edge pixels are near-neutral vs 7-9% on the references, which use tinted dark material tones), and only 13 distinct colours in total against 66-185 on the references. Its 11 visible tones per tile are close to the references' 10-12 and it has no flat fills, but the tone count comes from a tiny, simple object. It lacks per-tile highlights, grain and the multi-step ramps the references carry. The sticker-like outline and the shallow ramps outweigh the tone count.

surfaces.part: stair steps (treads as 1-row highlight lines, risers below)

answer.evidence: The lintel (rows 0-2) is a 3-row front-facing strip: a highlight at row 1 and a dark row at row 2, with no receding top plane. Each stair step is a 1-row bright edge line (rows 10, 13, 16, 19, 23, 28, 34...) over a 3-4 row riser face and a 2-row dark gap. The treads show no depth and read as a flat front elevation. The jambs are vertical faces. No ellipse, roof slope or visible contents give a real top surface of 3 or more rows.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small stairs-down prop (wooden stair frame with steps), not a whole building with roof, walls and door/windows, so it is not the same kind as the references. Its measured facts are 11 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10 for the references, and 0% near-flat coverage, so density on paper is comparable. However, 81% of its dark edge pixels are near-neutral, against 7% and 9% for the references, so it has the uniform near-black sticker outline instead of dark material-tone outlines. By eye, the wood ramps show only about 3 lightness steps (light plank, mid, dark) with a dark frame line, which is shallower than the 5-6 steps of the reference roofs and walls. There is no per-tile highlight or grain like the reference tile scallops and plaster speckle. The piece is also very small and sparse, so it looks flatter and more sticker-like beside the references. Fail on the near-black outline and shallow shading.

answer.evidence: The object is a doorway frame seen straight on, with a descending staircase inside. The lintel at rows 0-2 is a 3-row front-facing beam, with a light row at 1 and a dark row at 2. It has no sloped roof and no real horizontal band, so it is only a rim. The posts are vertical faces. Each step is a 1-row light highlight (rows 19, 23, 28, 34) over a wood riser face, so it is a front-facing strip with no tread surface. The bright bands at rows 10-16 are far steps, also seen face-on. Nothing shows a horizontal top surface of more than 2 rows, so the drawing reads as a flat front elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small wooden stairs-down prop, not a whole building with roof, walls and door/windows, so it is not the same kind as the references. On the measured facts it is close to the references: 11 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10, and 0% near-flat coverage. The outline is the problem. 81% of its dark edge pixels are near-neutral, against 7% and 9% for the references, so it has the uniform dark sticker line rather than a dark tone of the adjacent material. Its shading is shallow, about 4 steps on the wood planks and rails, against about 6 on the references' roof tiles and walls. The wood has some plank grain but lacks the per-tile highlights and speckle of the references. Overall it is a clean, small prop that falls short of the Beodeul standard on outline and shading depth.
